headline: Portugal closes all its schools for a big storm

sources.title: Portugal closes all schools and non-essential services due to a major Atlantic storm (AP)

Situação de alerta a 11 de novembro (Lexpoint)

chunks.text: On November 11, 2026, Portugal closed all of its [[roughly]] 8,000 schools because of a storm. It was the first time [[in living memory]] that schools across the country had closed over a [[storm forecast]]. The government also shut [[non-essential services]], public offices that people do not need in an emergency. It told everyone to {{stay in}}. Officials {{closed off}} beaches and [[riverside]] areas.

verbs.why: We stay in when it is very cold outside. Many families stay in on rainy weekends and watch movies. Portugal's government told everyone to stay in on November 11, 2026, as Storm Charles arrived.

verbs.correct: To stop people from entering a place
verbs.wrong: To give a place a new name
verbs.why: The police close off the street during the parade. Workers close off part of the park when they fix the paths. Officials in Portugal closed off beaches and riverside areas before the storm.

chunks.text: Portugal, a country in southwest Europe, {{geared up}} for Storm Charles on November 10. The government declared a [[state of alert]], an official warning level that lets it order special safety measures. [[Emergency services]] and army units were [[on standby]], ready to help. Portugal's prime minister {{headed up}} a [[crisis team]] with eight ministers. Forecasters warned of heavy rain and [[wind gusts]] of up to 93 miles per hour.

verbs.why: Stores gear up for the holiday season every November. The team gears up for the big game with extra practice. Portugal geared up for Storm Charles on November 10, the day before it hit.

verbs.correct: To lead a group or a team
verbs.wrong: To quit a job after a storm
verbs.why: A senior nurse heads up the night staff at the hospital. My aunt heads up the parents' group at our school. Portugal's prime minister headed up a crisis team with eight ministers during the storm.

chunks.text: Power {{went out}} for thousands of people on November 10. On November 11, more than 300 flights were canceled. In Lisbon, the capital, some streets flooded when [[drains]] {{backed up}}. Web Summit, a huge [[technology conference]] in Lisbon with about 70,000 visitors, {{called off}} its second day. The government said that day should not {{go ahead}} because of floods, transport problems and strong winds hitting [[outdoor structures]].

verbs.correct: To stop working or giving light
verbs.why: The lights go out when the wind gets very strong. In our old house, the power goes out every winter. Power went out for thousands of people in Portugal on November 10.

verbs.correct: To become blocked so water cannot flow
verbs.wrong: To get wider after heavy rain
verbs.why: The kitchen sink backs up when we pour oil down it. Old drains often back up after a big storm. Some streets in Lisbon flooded when drains backed up during Storm Charles.
Our school calls off the field trip when it rains. The town calls off the fireworks if the wind is too strong. Web Summit called off its second day in Lisbon because of the storm.

verbs.wrong: To be shown on live TV
verbs.why: The concert goes ahead even in light rain. Most weddings go ahead on the planned day. Portugal's government said the second day of Web Summit should not go ahead.

chunks.text: Forecasters said the storm had {{died down}} and was milder than feared. Wind gusts topped 75 miles per hour in places but did less damage than expected. By mid-afternoon, officials had {{scaled back}} the [[red alert]], the highest warning, from more than half the country to one southern region. In January 2026, the government faced [[harsh criticism]] for its [[weak response]] to Storm Kristin, which {{knocked down}} thousands of trees. The minister in charge of public safety {{brushed off}} claims that the government had [[overreacted]], saying it followed the forecast. The storm was expected to {{move on}} to Spain.

verbs.why: The wind usually dies down at night. The noise in the classroom dies down when the teacher walks in. Forecasters said Storm Charles had died down and was milder than feared.

verbs.correct: To make something smaller or less
verbs.wrong: To repeat something on the radio
verbs.why: Many companies scale back their plans when sales are slow. The city scales back bus service in the summer. Officials in Portugal scaled back the red alert to one southern region by mid-afternoon.

verbs.correct: To make something fall to the ground
verbs.wrong: To cut something into small pieces
verbs.why: Strong winds often knock down power lines. A big wave sometimes knocks down a fence near the beach. In January 2026, Storm Kristin knocked down thousands of trees in Portugal.

verbs.correct: To refuse to take something seriously
verbs.wrong: To print something on a sign
verbs.why: My brother brushes off every warning about his health. Some players brush off bad news and keep playing hard. Portugal's minister in charge of public safety brushed off claims that the government had overreacted.

verbs.correct: To leave and travel somewhere else
verbs.wrong: To become a big ocean wave
verbs.why: The circus moves on to a new town every week. Most summer storms move on after a few hours. After Portugal, Storm Charles was expected to move on to Spain.

mainIdea.s: Portugal shut all its schools and many public offices because a big storm was coming. The storm was milder than expected, and officials said they had not acted too strongly.
mainIdea.why: About 8,000 schools closed and people were told to stay in. The storm did less damage than expected, and a minister brushed off claims of overreacting.

mainIdea.s: A powerful Atlantic storm forced the country to close every classroom for a day. It caused far worse damage than earlier storms, so leaders now plan to keep schools shut for weeks.
mainIdea.why: Close, but forecasters said the storm had died down. It did less damage than expected, and nothing says schools will stay closed for weeks.

mainIdea.s: Portugal opened a new airport near Lisbon to handle more tourists next year. The project took ten years and should bring thousands of new jobs to the area around the capital.
mainIdea.why: This story is about a storm. Portugal closed its schools and public offices, and more than 300 flights were canceled.

lines.text: Did you see that Portugal closed every single school for a storm?
About 8,000 of them. The government told everyone to {{stay in}}, and officials {{closed off}} the beaches.
So Lisbon must have been [[a ghost town]].
Pretty much. Lots of flights were canceled, and some streets flooded when the drains {{backed up}}.
Was the storm as bad as they said?
No, it {{died down}} and was weaker than feared. By the afternoon, officials {{scaled back}} the red alert.
In January 2026, another storm {{knocked down}} thousands of trees, and people said the government was too slow.
So this time they weren't [[taking any chances]].
Exactly. Even that huge tech conference in Lisbon {{called off}} a whole day. The government said it shouldn't {{go ahead}}.
Who was in charge of all this?
The prime minister {{headed up}} a crisis team with eight ministers.
Wow. I bet some people think it was too much.
Some did. But the minister in charge of public safety {{brushed off}} that idea. He said they just followed the forecast.
Well, [[you can't win]]. Do too little, people get mad. Do too much, people get mad.
Right. And it's easy to [[second-guess]] them after the storm ends.
True. I'd rather have a quiet day at home than a tree on my car.

expressions.def: A place that is very quiet because almost nobody is there
ex: On Sunday morning, downtown is a ghost town.
During the snowstorm, the mall was a ghost town.

expressions.def: Used with 'not' to say someone is being very careful to avoid a risk
ex: The doctor isn't taking any chances, so she wants more tests.
We weren't taking any chances, so we left two hours early.

expressions.def: Used to say that people will complain whatever you do
ex: If I cook, it's too spicy. If I don't, they're hungry. You can't win.

expressions.def: To question a decision after it was made, often when it is too late
ex: Don't second-guess yourself. Your first answer was right.
Fans always second-guess the coach after a loss.
